slide_text: Inventing a Recommender System How does Netflix know what you should watch next? How does Spotify build your Discover Weekly? Nobody at those companies watches movies on your behalf and takes notes. The trick is beautifully simple: Find people whose taste matches yours, and recommend what they loved and you haven't seen yet. This is called collaborative filtering , and in this chapter you will invent it from scratch -- using real movie ratings collected from a live class of students. By the end you will compute, for any person in the class, the three movies they are most likely to enjoy. The plan: Clean the data -- real data is messy: missing ratings, people who barely rated anything, generous vs stingy raters. Measure taste similarity -- invent cosine similarity, then compute every pair of similarities in a single matrix multiplication. Recommend -- combine similarity with ratings to score unseen movies. Bonus -- how would this scale to Netflix size? Invent the MapReduce trick for multiplying gigantic sparse matrices. You'll need and . If you know a little pandas (reading a CSV, selecting columns) you're ready; we'll introduce everything else as we go. Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

slide_text: Quick Check -- Why Normalize Ratings? Before computing cosine similarity, you applied min-max scaling to each person's ratings. Why is this normalization step important? A. It makes the computation faster B. Without normalization, a generous rater (who gives 4s and 5s to everything) would appear similar to another generous rater even if their actual preferences are completely different C. Python requires values between 0 and 1 for cosine similarity D. It removes missing values from the matrix

fragments.text: Answer: B. Without normalization, people who rate on a similar scale look alike regardless of their actual tastes. Min-max scaling strips away the scale and keeps only the pattern of preferences.

slide_text: Part 3: Measuring Taste

How Similar Are Two People? Each person is now a column of 25 numbers -- a vector (just a list of numbers, one per movie). Two people with similar taste should have vectors pointing in a similar direction . You already know the dot product from the Secrets of Prediction chapter. Think about these questions: The dot product of two identical vectors is large. The dot product of vectors pointing in completely different directions (at right angles) is 0. So the dot product tells you something about alignment . But it also depends on how big the numbers are -- how can you remove that size effect? What if you divided the dot product by both vectors' lengths? What would that give you for identical vectors? For vectors at right angles? This quantity -- the dot product divided by the product of lengths -- is called cosine similarity : 1 means identical taste, 0 means completely unrelated taste. It measures direction only , which is one more defense against scale differences between raters. Your task: write for two columns of .

It starts with one observation: What happens to the similarity formula when both vectors already have length 1? Simplify the formula and see what's left. A vector divided by its own length has length 1 (called a unit vector ). When both vectors are unit vectors, the denominator is [math], so cosine similarity becomes just the dot product . slide_text: Quick Check -- The Cold Start Problem A brand-new user signs up and hasn't rated any movies yet. What happens when the recommender tries to find their taste twin? A. The system recommends the most popular movies by default B. Cosine similarity can't be computed -- the user's rating vector is all zeros (or NaN), so there's no direction to compare C. The system assigns random ratings and proceeds normally D. The user is automatically matched with the most active rater

fragments.text: Answer: B. With no ratings, the user's vector is all zeros or all NaN. A zero vector has no direction, so cosine similarity is undefined (you'd be dividing by zero). This is the famous cold-start problem -- it's why every streaming service asks new users to "pick a few titles you like" before showing recommendations.

slide_text: You just built a working collaborative-filtering recommender on real data. Try on a few more people -- do the suggestions make sense given who their taste twin is? One honest limitation to notice: what would do for a brand-new person with zero ratings? Nothing useful -- there's no vector to compare. This is the famous cold-start problem , and it's why every streaming service pesters new users to "pick a few titles you like" before showing recommendations.

slide_text: Quick Check -- User-User vs Item-Item You built two kinds of similarity: user-user () and item-item (). If Netflix has 300 million users but only 20,000 movies, which approach produces a smaller, more manageable similarity table? A. User-user, because users are more important than movies B. Item-item, because a 20,000 x 20,000 table is much smaller than a 300-million x 300-million table -- and movie similarities change less often than user preferences C. Both produce the same size table D. Neither -- you need a completely different algorithm at that scale

fragments.text: Answer: B. A 20,000 x 20,000 item-item table has 400 million entries -- large but feasible. A 300M x 300M user-user table would have 90 quadrillion entries -- impossible to even store. Plus, movie taste profiles are more stable than individual user behavior, so the item-item table doesn't need constant recomputation.

slide_text: Part 6: Scaling to Netflix -- MapReduce Matrix Multiplication Our class matrix was 25 x 15. Netflix has around 300 million users and 20,000 titles. The user-similarity matrix alone would have [math] entries -- no single computer can even hold that, let alone compute it. Two observations rescue us: The matrix is almost entirely zeros (it is "sparse"). A typical user rates a few dozen titles out of 20,000. Why store the zeros at all? Keep only the non-zero entries as triples -- like a list of receipts instead of a massive spreadsheet with mostly blank cells. Matrix multiplication breaks down into tiny independent jobs. Recall: the result entry at row [math], column [math] is a sum of products. Each non-zero pair contributes one product to one output cell -- and every contribution can be computed on a different machine , then summed up per cell at the end. That "compute little pieces anywhere, then group and add by key" pattern is called MapReduce , and it's how the tech giants handle these enormous computations.

Sparse MapReduce Matrix Multiplication Your task: write where each argument is a list of triples representing the non-zero entries. Return a dict mapping for the non-zero entries of the product. The key insight: for every non-zero entry and every non-zero entry that share the same middle index , you get one contribution to the output cell . Collect all such contributions and sum them per output cell.

slide_text: Part 7: What You Invented This is collaborative filtering -- recommending purely from the pattern of who-likes-what, knowing nothing about the movies themselves (no genres, no actors, no plots). The alternative, content-based filtering , compares movie features instead; modern systems blend both. And that trick -- all-pairs similarity as a single matrix product -- will meet you again in the most unexpected place: it's the heart of the attention mechanism inside large language models (the AI behind ChatGPT and similar tools), where every word in a sentence computes its similarity to every other word. Same math, different vectors.
